cards.title: Europe in 1914
cards.explanation: In 1914 Europe was led by a few powerful empires, including Britain, France, Germany, Russia and Austria-Hungary. They competed for land, trade and influence. Historians often sum up the long-term causes of the war with the word MAIN.
keyPoints: A handful of great powers dominated Europe
They competed for land, trade and power
MAIN stands for militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism
cards.rememberThis: MAIN names the four long-term causes: militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism.

cards.title: Militarism
cards.explanation: Militarism means building up armed forces and trusting them to solve problems. Germany and Britain raced to build bigger navies, especially huge battleships called dreadnoughts. Countries also made detailed war plans, like Germany's Schlieffen Plan.
keyPoints: Armies and navies grew fast before 1914
Britain and Germany had a naval race
Ready-made war plans made fighting start fast
cards.rememberThis: An arms race left the great powers ready, and quick, to fight.

cards.title: Alliances
cards.explanation: The great powers split into two groups that promised to defend each other. The Triple Alliance joined Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. The Triple Entente joined France, Russia and Britain. These promises meant a small conflict could pull in many countries.
keyPoints: Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy
Triple Entente: France, Russia and Britain
Alliances could turn a local war into a world war
cards.rememberThis: Alliances meant one country's war could drag its partners in.

cards.title: Imperialism
cards.explanation: Imperialism is when a country builds an empire by taking control of other lands. Britain and France held huge empires, and Germany wanted one too. Competition for colonies in Africa and Asia created jealousy and distrust.
keyPoints: Empires brought wealth, resources and status
Germany felt left behind in the race for colonies
Rivalry over colonies raised tension
cards.rememberThis: Competition for colonies made the great powers suspicious of each other.

cards.title: Nationalism
cards.explanation: Nationalism is strong pride in your own nation, sometimes with the belief that it is better than others. It made many people eager to support a war. In the Balkans, Slavic groups like the Serbs wanted freedom from Austria-Hungary.
keyPoints: Pride in the nation made war popular
Serbia wanted to unite Slavic peoples
Austria-Hungary saw Serbian nationalism as a threat
cards.rememberThis: Nationalism made war popular and made the Balkans explosive.

cards.title: The assassination in Sarajevo
cards.explanation: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was shot in Sarajevo. The killer, Gavrilo Princip, was a young Bosnian Serb helped by a secret Serbian nationalist group called the Black Hand. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia.
keyPoints: Franz Ferdinand was killed on 28 June 1914
Gavrilo Princip was helped by the Black Hand
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia
cards.rememberThis: The killing of Franz Ferdinand was the spark that started the war.

cards.title: How one shot became a world war
cards.explanation: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, with Germany's support. Russia mobilized to protect Serbia, so Germany declared war on Russia and then on France. When Germany marched through neutral Belgium, Britain declared war on 4 August 1914.
keyPoints: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia
Alliances pulled in Russia, Germany and France
Germany invading Belgium brought Britain in
cards.rememberThis: Within weeks, the alliance system turned one murder into a world war.

quiz.question: What does the M in MAIN stand for?
quiz.explanation: MAIN stands for militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism.

quiz.question: Which countries formed the Triple Entente?
quiz.explanation: The Triple Entente joined France, Russia and Britain.

quiz.question: What was the naval race before the war?
options: Britain and Germany competing to build bigger navies
A sailing race between royal families
quiz.explanation: Britain and Germany raced to build more and bigger battleships.

quiz.question: Who was assassinated in Sarajevo in June 1914?
quiz.explanation: Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary.

quiz.question: Why did Austria-Hungary see Serbia as a threat?
options: Serbian nationalism encouraged Slavs to break away
Serbia was part of the Triple Alliance
quiz.explanation: Serbian nationalism encouraged Slavic peoples inside Austria-Hungary to want independence.

quiz.question: What finally brought Britain into the war?
quiz.explanation: Britain had promised to protect Belgium, so the German invasion brought Britain in.
